content: The study by CJ Humphreys et al. was conducted in the United Kingdom and involved families with children under the age of five living in housing provided by the Glasgow Housing Association (GHA). The study was a randomized trial that included an economic evaluation. Families were eligible if they lived in GHA-provided housing and had children under five, but were excluded if they were moving out of the property, had unsuitable pipework for thermostatic mixing valve (TMV) installation, or were participating in other tap water scald prevention projects. Recruitment involved written invitations sent to tenants identified through the East End Child Safety Project database or the GHA tenant database, as well as face-to-face contact with local housing organizations. The intervention group consisted of 124 families who received an educational leaflet about TMVs before installation. A TMV, set to a maximum temperature of 45°C, was installed by a qualified plumber, and a waterproof educational guide on using the TMV was attached to the tap. The control group received the same intervention after the study follow-up was completed. The results showed a significant reduction in the risk of severe scalds after TMV installation. The risk of a child requiring hospitalization for five or more days or treatment at a burns center decreased from 1 in 3,964 to 1 in 12,398. The risk of shorter hospitalizations decreased from 1 in 5,250 to 1 in 16,186, and the risk of emergency department attendance decreased from 1 in 1,475 to 1 in 4,625. Overall, the risk of total emergency department visits or admissions decreased from 1 in 892 to 1 in 2,788. These findings were based on data from the original randomized controlled trial and estimates of emergency department visits for bath water scalds derived from UK data sources. The systematic review by Kendrick et al. (2012) focused on home safety education and the provision of safety equipment for injury prevention. It included randomized controlled trials, non-randomized trials, and controlled before-and-after studies involving children and young people under 19 years of age and their families. Interventions included home safety education with or without safety equipment such as stair gates, fireguards, smoke alarms, and window locks. Outcomes included self-reported or medically attended injuries, possession and use of safety equipment, and safety practices. The review included 98 studies and found some evidence that home safety interventions improved the possession and use of safety equipment but did not consistently reduce injury rates. Interventions providing free or low-cost safety equipment were more effective in improving safety practices. The review by Turner et al. (2011) examined home modifications to reduce injuries. It included 29 randomized trials involving people of all ages living in homes subject to housing regulations. Interventions included modifications such as grab rails, stair gates, fireguards, and hot-water tap adaptations. The review found insufficient evidence to determine whether these interventions reduced injuries, particularly in studies focusing on children or older adults. The review by McClure et al. (2005) evaluated population-based interventions to prevent fall-related injuries in older adults. It included six community trials and found decreases in fall-related injuries ranging from 6% to 33%. The review by DiGuiseppi et al. (2001) assessed interventions promoting smoke alarm ownership and functionality. It included 26 studies, 17 of which were randomized. While these programs modestly increased smoke alarm ownership and functionality, they did not demonstrate a beneficial effect on fire-related injuries or fires. The review by Gates et al. (2008) focused on multifactorial assessments and targeted interventions to prevent falls and injuries among older adults in community and emergency care settings. It included 19 studies and found a reduction in fall-related injuries but no significant differences in hospital admissions, emergency department attendance, or mortality. The review by Neyens et al. (2011) examined interventions to prevent falls in elderly residents of long-term care facilities. It included 20 trials and found significant reductions in fall rates (27% to 49%) and recurrent fallers (19%). Effective interventions included vitamin D supplementation, clinical medication reviews, and multifactorial approaches such as safety assessments, environmental adaptations, and balance training. The review by Chang et al. (2004) analyzed interventions for fall prevention in older adults. It included 40 trials and found that multifactorial interventions, exercise, environmental modifications, and education reduced the rate of falls, with eight fewer falls per 100 patients per month.
